12.1.summary:
Everything you hope to reach some day by a long detour is available now, if you stop denying it to yourself. Let go of the past, leave the future to providence, and handle the present well: accept your lot as something made for you, and be honest and fair with everyone, giving each person their due.

Don't let other people's bad behaviour, gossip or bodily discomfort knock you off course. What should frighten you near the end isn't dying, but never having really started to live by reason. Do that and you stop feeling like a stranger in your own world, surprised by everything.
12.1.today: Think of the person who plans to be calm and kind once the house move, the promotion or the kids' exams are over. Marcus's point is that the patience you're saving for later is available on this morning's commute, in how you answer the next awkward email.

12.2.summary: God, as Marcus pictures it, looks straight at people's minds, ignoring bodies, clothes and appearances. If you practise seeing yourself and others the same way, a lot of worry falls away. Someone who doesn't fuss over the body wrapped around their mind isn't going to fret about clothes, houses, reputation or putting on a show.
12.2.today: Before a party or an interview, notice how much energy goes into the outfit, the tidy flat behind you on the video call or the right photo for your profile. Marcus would ask what the person is like underneath all that, including you.

12.3.summary:
You're made of three things: a body, the breath of life, and a mind. You look after the first two, but only the mind is really yours. So separate it from everything it can't control: what others say and do, your own past words and deeds, worries about the future, bodily sensations, and the general whirl of events.

Then the mind can stand free, act justly, accept what happens and tell the truth. Marcus borrows an image from Empedocles, the early Greek philosopher who pictured the perfect cosmos as a sphere at rest. Live only in the present, which is the only life you actually have, and you'll spend what time remains calm and true to the reason within you.
12.3.today: Lying awake replaying something you said at dinner, then worrying about tomorrow's meeting, while your back aches, is the mind tangled in all the things Marcus says to peel off. The bit left over, deciding what to do now, is the part that's really yours.

12.4.summary: It's odd: we each love ourselves more than anyone, yet we care more about what others think of us than what we think of ourselves. Marcus tests it with a thought experiment. If someone ordered you to say every thought out loud the moment you had it, you couldn't stand it for a day. That shows how much we're living for the neighbours' opinion rather than our own judgement.
12.4.today: Notice how quickly a post gets deleted when it doesn't get many likes, or how you'll redo an outfit because of what a colleague might say, even though you liked it. Yet you'd happily ignore your own private verdict that you were short with someone this morning.

12.5.summary:
Marcus raises a hard question: if the gods arranged everything so well for humans, why let the very best people, those closest to the divine, simply vanish for good at death? He doesn't pretend to have an answer.

Instead he reasons that if it would have been right for them to survive, the gods would have made it so, because what is just is also possible for them. The fact that he can even put this complaint to the gods assumes they are good and fair, and good and fair gods wouldn't leave something unjust in the universe. So, if this is how things are, it must be how they ought to be.

12.6.summary: Keep practising even what you think you'll never manage. Marcus's example is the left hand: clumsy at most tasks, yet it holds a horse's reins more firmly than the right, simply because that's the job it has been trained for. Skill comes from repetition, not from natural talent.
12.6.today: Learning a language at forty, playing the guitar with stiff fingers, or staying patient with a teenager can all feel hopeless at first. They're like the left hand on the reins: awkward until you've done it enough times that it becomes the thing you're steadiest at.

12.7.summary: A note to himself with three things to think about: what state of body and mind you'd want to be in when death arrives, how short life is against the vast stretch of time on either side, and how fragile everything material is. Each thought shrinks petty concerns down to size.

12.8.summary: A checklist for seeing clearly. Look at things with their wrapping removed and ask what actions are really aiming at. Think about what pain, pleasure, death and fame amount to. Notice that people cause their own distress, that no one can block another from acting well, and that so much comes down to how we see things.
12.8.today: When a rejection email lands, strip it back: it's some words on a screen, and the sting comes from what you tell yourself about them. The same goes for a sharp comment in a meeting, which can't stop you behaving well unless you let it.

12.9.summary: Hold your principles like an all-in wrestler, not a gladiator. The pancratiast fought with hands and feet, so could never be disarmed, while a gladiator who drops his sword is finished. Your values should be part of you, always ready, not a tool you can fumble in a crisis.
12.9.today: It's easy to know the theory of staying calm while reading a book on a Sunday. The test is the burnt dinner, the delayed train or the rude customer, when there's no time to go and fetch your principles. They need to be already in your hands.

12.10.summary: A brief method for seeing anything as it really is: break it into what it's made of, what shape or pattern makes it the thing it is, and what it's for. Taking things apart like this drains away the glamour or dread we pile onto them and leaves the plain facts.

12.11.summary: Marcus marvels at how much power a person has: the power to do only what God would approve, and to accept whatever God sends. Both are entirely within your reach. You can always choose to act well, and you can always welcome what happens rather than fighting it.

12.12.summary: There's no one to blame for what happens in the natural course of things. Not the gods, who never do wrong, and not people, who only do wrong out of ignorance rather than real intent. Blame has no proper target, so let it go.
12.12.today: When a holiday is ruined by storms, there's nothing to rage at. When a flatmate leaves the kitchen in a state, they're probably not plotting against you, just careless or unaware. Dropping the urge to find a culprit saves a lot of energy.

12.13.summary: Being surprised by anything that happens in life is ridiculous, Marcus says, and it marks you out as a stranger in the world. Illness, loss, rudeness and setbacks are all part of the ordinary run of things. Someone who understands how the world works expects them and isn't knocked flat when they arrive.

12.14.summary:
Marcus lays out three possibilities: the universe runs on fixed fate, or on a kindly providence that can respond to us, or it's just a purposeless chaos. Each one points to the same calm. If fate is fixed, why struggle against it? If providence listens, make yourself worth helping. If it's chaos, be glad you have a reasoning mind inside you amid the storm.

Even if the storm sweeps you away, it can only take your body and breath. It can't take your mind's ability to judge well.

12.15.summary: A lamp keeps shining brightly right up until it's put out. Marcus asks why the truth, fairness and self-control inside you should go dark before you die. He's challenging himself to keep his character burning at full strength to the end, rather than letting it fade with age, tiredness or circumstance.

12.16.summary:
When someone seems to have done wrong, slow down. Do you actually know it was wrong? And if it was, they may already be judging themselves harshly, which is like scratching at their own face. Expecting a bad person never to act badly is as silly as expecting figs without juice, babies who don't cry or horses that don't neigh.

People with that character will behave that way. If you're going to be sharp about it, put that energy into helping change their disposition, not into getting angry.
12.16.today: When the driver cuts you up or a relative makes the usual tactless remark, ask first whether you've read it right. Then remember that getting outraged when someone acts exactly as they always do is like being shocked that a toddler cried on a plane.

12.17.summary: Two short rules: if it isn't right, don't do it, and if it isn't true, don't say it. The text breaks off after this, probably damaged in the surviving manuscript, but the core is complete. Much of ethical life can be steered by these two tests applied in the moment.
12.17.today: Before forwarding the juicy rumour, ask whether it's true. Before quietly fudging the expenses or a timesheet, ask whether it's right. If the answer is no, that settles it, however small the matter feels.

12.18.summary: Whenever something makes a strong impression on you, break it down: what kind of thing it is, what it's made of, what it's for, and how long it will last. Most strong reactions shrink once you see a thing in parts and remember that it's temporary.
12.18.today: A glowing review of a gadget you suddenly need, or a scary headline, can be taken apart the same way. It's plastic and metal, it does one job, and it'll be out of date in two years. The headline is words chosen to grab you, and next week it will be forgotten.

12.19.summary: You have something better and more divine in you than the passions that jerk you about like a puppet on strings: your reasoning mind. Marcus then models the habit he recommends, stopping to ask what's in his mind right now. Is it fear, suspicion, desire?
12.19.today: Halfway through an angry reply to a message, or reaching for the phone for the tenth time in an hour, pause and name what's pulling the strings. Is it worry about being left out, irritation, or craving? Naming it often loosens its grip.

12.20.summary: Two rules for action. First, don't do anything at random or without a reason. Second, make sure what you do is aimed at the common good, the benefit of the people around you, and not only at yourself. For the Stoics, humans are made to live and work together, so acting for others is acting according to our nature.
12.20.today: Before saying yes to another project, or spending an evening drifting between apps, ask what it's for. And when you do act, ask who else it helps: the team, the family, the neighbour who could use a hand with the shopping.

12.21.summary: Before long you'll be no one and nowhere. Nothing you see now will remain, and neither will anyone alive today. This isn't meant as despair. Everything is built to change, transform and pass away so that new things can follow in an unbroken chain, and you're part of that same process.

12.22.summary: Much of what disturbs you is your opinion about events, and your opinions are under your control. Drop the opinion whenever you like and, like a sailor who has rounded a headland out of the wind, you'll find calm water and a still bay. The storm was in your judgement, not in the situation.
12.22.today: A colleague's curt one-line email can ruin an afternoon if you decide it means they're annoyed with you. Let go of that story, and it's just a short email from someone busy. The calm was there all along.

12.23.summary:
Any single activity that stops at its proper time suffers nothing bad by stopping, and neither does the person doing it. Your life is just the sum of all your activities, so the same goes for it. When it ends at its due time, nothing bad has happened to you.

Nature sets that time, through old age or otherwise, and nature renews the universe by changing its parts. Death is out of your control, so it isn't shameful, and it serves the whole, so it's actually good. Accepting it means moving in step with the divine order.

12.24.summary:
Three principles to keep ready. First, act only with thought and fairness, and don't blame chance or providence for what happens to you from outside. Second, remember what every living thing is: where it comes from, what it's made of and what it breaks down into.

Third, imagine being lifted high above the earth and looking down at all human life, in its variety and among countless other beings. Every time you looked, you'd see the same things: the same patterns and the same short lives. Is any of that worth being proud of?

12.25.summary: Throw away your opinion and you're saved. So who's stopping you? Marcus means that our distress comes from the judgements we add to events, and dropping those judgements is something only we can do, and something no one can prevent us from doing.

12.26.summary:
Whenever you're upset, you've forgotten something. Everything happens according to the way the universe works. Another person's wrongdoing is their business, not a harm to you. Things have always happened like this and always will. You're closely related to every human being, not by blood but by sharing in reason.

You've also forgotten that each person's mind comes from the divine, that nothing, not even your child, body or soul, is truly owned, that so much rests on opinion, and that you only ever live, and only ever lose, the present moment.
12.26.today: After a row with a sibling or a stinging comment from your boss, run down Marcus's list. Usually you'll find you've forgotten at least one thing, perhaps that their behaviour is theirs to answer for, or that you're only losing this moment if you keep chewing it over.

12.27.summary:
Keep in mind the people who were famous for raging about something, or for great glory, disaster, feuds or luck. Where are they now? Smoke, ash, a story, or not even a story. Marcus lists men of his world known for their grand retreats and estates, including the emperor Tiberius, who withdrew to Capri. All that effort and pride came to nothing.

Far better to use whatever chances you get to be fair, self-controlled and reverent, simply and without fuss. The worst kind of pride is being proud of how humble you are.
12.27.today: Think of the influencer everyone talked about five years ago, the office feud nobody can now explain, or the person who makes a show of how unpretentious their holiday was. All of it fades. What lasts is how decently you treated people along the way.

12.28.summary: When asked how he knows the gods exist without having seen them, Marcus gives two answers. First, they can be seen, which reflects the ancient belief that the sun, moon and stars were divine. Second, he has never seen his own soul either, yet he respects it. He knows the gods exist from constantly experiencing their power in the world, and that is enough for him to honour them.

12.29.summary: Living safely means examining everything thoroughly, seeing what it is, what it's made of and what gives it its form, and then putting your whole heart into acting fairly and speaking truthfully. What's left after that is to enjoy life by linking one good action to the next, with no gaps in between.
12.29.today: A good day can be built from small things done well, one after another: an honest answer to a client, a patient bedtime story, a fair split of the chores. Marcus's idea of enjoying life is stringing these together so closely that there's no room for the bad.

12.30.summary:
Sunlight is one light, even though walls and mountains break it into patches. Matter is one substance spread across countless bodies, and soul is one life shared among countless creatures. The same goes for mind: there's one reasoning soul, even if it looks divided between individuals.

Lifeless things like air and stone feel nothing for one another, though even they are held together. But minds are drawn to other minds in a special way. That pull towards fellowship with other reasoning beings is something that can't be broken.

12.31.summary: What exactly do you want when you want to keep living? To keep sensing, moving, growing, then declining, talking, thinking? Look at each of these and ask whether it's really worth craving. If you can see that they don't count for much, turn to what's left: following reason and God. And it makes no sense to honour reason while being upset that death will take away the lesser things.

12.32.summary: Each of us gets a tiny sliver of endless time, quickly swallowed by eternity, a tiny share of all matter and of the universal soul, and a tiny clod of earth to crawl about on. Seeing this, treat nothing as great except acting as your own nature leads you and bearing what nature as a whole brings. Marcus isn't belittling life, just putting status and possessions in proportion.

12.33.summary: The question that matters most is how your mind uses itself: how you judge, choose and respond. Everything depends on that. Everything else, whether it's in your control or not, is just lifeless ash and smoke by comparison. For Marcus, the quality of your own thinking and choosing is the only thing of real worth.

12.34.summary: Here is a strong argument for not fearing death: even people who believe pleasure is good and pain is bad, such as the Epicureans, have still looked down on death. If those who prize comfort above all can face it calmly, someone who cares mainly about character has even less reason to be afraid.

12.35.summary: Death holds no terror for someone who thinks only what comes at the right time is good, and who doesn't mind whether they do more or fewer good actions, or watch the world for longer or shorter. If acting well is what matters, length of life stops being the point.

12.36.summary:
Marcus closes the book by talking to himself directly. You've been a citizen of this great city, the world. Does it matter whether for five years or three? Nature, not a tyrant or a corrupt judge, brought you in and now sends you out.

It's like an actor dismissed by the official who hired him. You object that you've only played three acts of five, but in life three acts can be the whole play. The one who made you decides when the drama is complete, and you decided neither its beginning nor its end. So leave contentedly, because the one releasing you does so with goodwill.
